context.history: Arctic exploration and the search for a Northwest Passage were major public dreams in the early 1800s. Letters were a popular novel form (the epistolary novel).

significance: Walton is Victor's double: an ambitious man willing to risk others for discovery. The frame narrative invites readers to judge whether he will learn from Victor.

items.prompt: Which literary element does this describe in “Letter I”? Walton is ardent, self-educated and lonely; his ambition is described in the same glowing language Victor will use. Mark his superlatives.

Which literary element does this describe in “Letter I”? The novel opens in letters from Robert Walton to his sister Margaret Saville. The epistolary form makes us readers of private letters and puts a listener (Margaret, and us) at the edge of the story.

Evaluate this claim about the chapter: “Walton is introduced as a mirror for Victor, so the novel's warning about ambition begins before Victor appears.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.
items.expected: The claim is persuasive only in part. In support, “I shall satiate my ardent curiosity with the sight of a part of the world never before visited” (Letter I, paragraph 2) bears it out: His dream of a land "never before visited" and his heart that glows with enthusiasm use the same fevered vocabulary Victor will use about creating life, which invites readers to compare the two men. But “I feel my heart glow with an enthusiasm which elevates me to heaven” (Letter I, paragraph 3) complicates it, because here the text shows religious, heightened language for exploration; compare later with Victor's rapture. So the claim holds only once it is qualified: it explains much of the chapter, but it has to account for that passage too, which it does not do on its own.

I read “You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil…” slowly and put it in my own words: Walton writes to Margaret that no disaster has struck at the start of his voyage, though she feared it would. Next, craft. I notice the formal, slightly defensive tone, as if he expects to be scolded. The strongest word is “forebodings”: it reminds us that someone who loves him fears this expedition. Then, effect. Why does Walton begin by reassuring his sister? My answer: Walton begins by reassuring his sister because she had warned against his voyage; his eager confidence brushes aside warnings and mirrors Victor's, setting up the novel's warning about dangerous ambition.
